description: We are team Wilddd, building Pahiro: a flood and landslide watch for Nepal built on Synthetic Aperture Radar. When monsoon cloud blinds every optical satellite, radar still sees the ground. We combine SAR physics, a U-Net segmentation model and a clean web viewer, grounded in real Sentinel-1 data and aimed at NISAR, to turn radar backscatter into maps people can act on during a disaster.
summary: Pahiro is a flood and landslide watch for Nepal built on Synthetic Aperture Radar. During the 26 to 29 September 2024 floods, which killed more than 240 people across central Nepal, thick monsoon cloud blinded the optical satellites that most disaster maps rely on. Radar sends its own microwave pulse, so it sees the ground through cloud, smoke and darkness, and smooth floodwater shows up dark because it reflects the beam away from the satellite. We built a live web viewer that streams real Sentinel-1 radar of the Kathmandu Valley from before and after the flood, on the same orbit, so the water is visible in a single swipe. Behind it is a pipeline that selects comparable scenes, maps new water with a change-detection baseline, and trains a U-Net segmentation model on the Sen1Floods11 radar benchmark for Nepal terrain. It answers the challenge by turning SAR physics into a tool that a district officer can open on a phone during a disaster, and it is designed to run on NISAR data as it becomes available.
details:
What it does. Pahiro turns Synthetic Aperture Radar into flood and landslide maps for Nepal, for the hours when monsoon cloud hides the ground from optical satellites. The live viewer shows two real Sentinel-1 passes over the Kathmandu Valley, 20 September 2024 (calm) and 02 October 2024 (after the floods), on the same descending orbit so every pixel lines up. Drag the slider and the flooded river basin turns dark.

How it works. SAR satellites send their own microwave pulse and record the echo, so cloud, smoke and night do not stop them. Smooth standing water reflects the pulse away from the satellite, so flooded ground loses backscatter and appears dark. Our pipeline searches the Sentinel-1 archive through the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API, picks a before and after pair on one orbit, converts VV backscatter to decibels, and maps new water with an Otsu change-detection baseline. For the main model we train a ResNet34 U-Net on two-band (VV, VH) input using the Sen1Floods11 hand-labelled radar flood benchmark, then fine-tune it on Nepal terrain, so it can find water in a single post-event scene with no clean before image.

Benefits and goals. Disaster responders in Nepal currently wait days for a clear optical image. Radar is available within days of every pass, in any weather, for free. Our goal is a map a district officer or volunteer can open on a phone during the event, then crossed with population and road data to show who is cut off. The same pipeline is built to run on NISAR, the NASA-ISRO radar mission, which adds 12-day global coverage.

What is real today. Shipped: the live radar viewer and reproducible scene selection. In progress: the baseline flood mask overlay. Next: the trained U-Net and the population and road impact layer. We state this plainly so judges know exactly what is built.

Tools. Next.js, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS, Python, PyTorch, segmentation-models-pytorch, rasterio, scikit-image, the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC and tile APIs, deployed on Vercel.

SI acknowledgment. AI coding and writing assistants helped us research, write and debug the code, design the site and slides, and draft this text. All radar imagery is real Sentinel-1 data, not generated. This is also noted in the project README.
